sweep_summary: Burmese (nucl1310) is in the catalog as 'tonal' on Okell 1969. Three title hits: (1) Ozerov 2020 (LTBA, DOI 10.1075/ltba.20009.oze) is closed access (Unpaywall closed; GBP 15 at jbe-platform); its abstract describes phrase-level intonational accent placed by information structure in 'this tonal language' — prosody, not word stress; medium priority to acquire. (2) Green 1995 (Cornell WPCPL 10, ROA-115) downloaded open from roa.rutgers.edu and read; its 2005 revision (PL 570, DOI 10.15144/PL-570.1) downloaded open from the ANU repository (CC BY-SA) and from ROA-551: Burmese foot = one tone-bearing major syllable, minor schwa syllables unfooted and never word-final, 'tone-bearing syllables fill the role of stressed syllables' (ROA-115 p. 13) — refines, does not contradict, the tonal coding. (3) Than Than Win 2003 (SEALS VII, pp. 225-241) downloaded from the SEALang SALA archive (image-only; scanned sequentially at 300 dpi): about Burmese-accented English, with one aside that Burmese syllables receive equal stress (p. 231) — confirms no differential word stress. Also re-read Watkins 2001 JIPA (already held by the project): 'Stress is subordinate to tone in Burmese' (p. 293). No source found that supersedes Okell 1969; Green 1995/2005 is the best new first-hand statement.

new_statements.reading: Burmese has no word-stress system independent of tone. Prominence belongs to tone-bearing major (heavy) syllables, each of which is its own foot; toneless schwa minor syllables are unfooted and never word-final, so a word's final syllable is always a tone-bearing major syllable. Because (L L) feet do not exist, the foot's headedness (trochaic vs iambic) cannot be determined from stress placement (Green 2005 later calls it left-headed on mora-internal grounds). This agrees with Watkins 2001 p. 293 ('Stress is subordinate to tone in Burmese') and with the catalog's 'tonal' coding; it refines it by giving the foot/word-shape account of which syllables are prominent (major, tone-bearing) and which are reduced (schwa minor syllables).

tone_statements.quote: Burmese has eight monophthongs [a, i, u, e, ɛ, o, ɔ, ə], four diphthongs [aj, ej, ow, aw], and four tones [á, à, a̰, aʔ] (high, low, creaky, and checked). Major syllables may contain any vowel except [ə]; they may be open or closed, but only [ʔ] and placeless N can close a syllable; they must bear tone; and they may have simple (C) or complex (CG) onsets (G = glide). Minor syllables in Burmese contain only [ə]. They never involve codas, tone, or complex onsets.

sources.note: First-hand theoretical analysis: Burmese has no stress system separate from tone; the tone-bearing major (heavy) syllable is the foot and plays the role of the stressed syllable, while minor schwa syllables are unfooted (NON-FOOT(schwa)) and every word must end in a major syllable (ALIGN-R). Whether the (H) foot is trochaic or iambic is undecidable because (L L) feet do not exist (p. 13). Polysyllabic words of several major syllables are several feet/prosodic words, i.e. no single culminative word stress is posited.

sources.quote: 8. The tones are four: stop, creaky, heavy, and level. All syllables have tone except 'weak syllables', i.e. those with the vowel [schwa]. The presence of this vowel is therefore an indication of a toneless syllable. Toneless syllables are always prefixed to a syllable with tone. Stop tone occurs only in syllables with the final consonant ', and these syllables do not occur with any other tone. [...] All other syllables may have creaky, heavy, or level tone. (1.8, p. 5) | 15. Tones. Level tone: begins on a low pitch relative to the other three tones, and often remains level, but may rise (e.g. before a pause), or fall slightly (e.g. at the end of a sentence); normal voice-quality. The other three tones begin on a high pitch relative to level tone, but may fall (e.g. before level tone or at the end of a sentence). The difference between level tone and these three high tones sometimes sounds like stress to English ears: cf. convict (verb: low-high) and convict (noun: high-low). [...] Heavy tone: normal voice-quality, sometimes sounding almost breathy in contrast to creaky and stop tones. Creaky tone: glottally constricted ('creaky') voice-quality, i.e. a gradually applied glottal sto

sources.quote: You will notice that in Burmese the inflection of the voice determines the meaning of what is said. English is like that. We can say [it's] cold? or it's cold! sources.quote: Burmese has eight monophthongs [a, i, u, e, ɛ, o, ɔ, ə], four diphthongs [aj, ej, ow, aw], and four tones [á, à, a̰, aʔ] (high, low, creaky, and checked). Major syllables may contain any vowel except [ə]; they may be open or closed, but only [ʔ] and placeless N can close a syllable; they must bear tone; and they may have simple (C) or complex (CG) onsets (G = glide). Minor syllables in Burmese contain only [ə]. They never involve codas, tone, or complex onsets.

tone.quote: Just such a trace element exists in the so-called ‘creaky tone' of Burmese: ?auk mrac! … The tone and its statistical distribution. Within Modern Burmese, three tones are found in non-stopped syllables: the level tone, the "heavy' tone [hre?pauk], and the creaky tone [?auk mrac]. The creaky tone is by far the least frequently occurring Burmese tone (only about 350 words are found under ?auk mrac) but it is now scattered through the Modern Burmese lexicon. It is found as the lexical tone of at least some members of every word class

tone.quote: Tone-Pattern I. Burmese Tone 3 (Level Rising) usually corresponds to Tone 4 in P'u-t'ao Lisu … Tone-Pattern II. Burmese Tone 4 (Released Falling), while generally corresponding to Tone 5 in Lisu, may cover all three Even Tones in both dialects … Tone-Pattern III. Burmese Tone 2 (Short Falling). This tone is often indicated in Old Burmese script, but the words, though common, are few compared to those in the two other tones. … Stops. These, in Burmese, are not tonally significant; and since they end abruptly are, ipso facto, difficult to fit into a tonal system.
